I'll systematically compare the source against the draft, hunting for signature failures.

**Key passages to check:**

1. "Never a tone of arrogance! Never a gesture of pride!" — The draft quotes this with quotation marks, treating it as a quotation from somewhere, when in the source it is Adams's own rhetorical declaration. This is a minor distortion but the phrasing is preserved.

2. The passage about Charles Francis Adams's character — "a balance of mind and temper that neither challenged nor avoided notice, nor admitted question of superiority or inferiority, of jealousy, of personal motives, from any source, even under great pressure" — this is flattened/absent in the draft.

3. The passage on Dana: "it was aristocratic to the tenth generation" — present.

4. The Sumner passage: "his solitude was glacial" — present.

5. The critical passage: "That the most powerful emotion of man, next to the sexual, should disappear...seemed to him the most curious social phenomenon he had to account for in a long life" — present verbatim.

6. The passage: "The passionate hatred of school methods was almost a method in itself" — present.

7. "He always reckoned his school-days, from ten to sixteen years old, as time thrown away" — present.

8. The happiest hours passage — present verbatim.

9. The crucial interpretive passage about Charles Francis Adams's poise: "a balance of mind and temper that neither challenged nor avoided notice, nor admitted question of superiority or inferiority, of jealousy, of personal motives, from any source, even under great pressure. This unusual poise of judgment and temper, ripened by age, became the more striking to his son Henry as he learned to measure the mental faculties themselves" — this is significantly flattened in the draft.

10. "The world never loved perfect poise. What the world does love is commonly absence of poise, for it has to be amused. Napoleons and Andrew Jacksons amuse it, but it is not amused by perfect balance." — The draft compresses this to "The world never loved perfect poise; it loves absence of it, for it must be amused." The specific Napoleons and Andrew Jacksons line is dropped.

11. The Sumner passage about his model's "superiority which defied imitation. To the twelve-year-old boy, his father, Dr. Palfrey, Mr. Dana, were men, more or less like what he himself might become; but Mr. Sumner was a different order—heroic." — "heroic" is present, but the key contrast (father/Palfrey/Dana as men vs. Sumner as different order) is condensed.

12. The Dana description: "a direct, rather bluff, vigorous seaman, and only as one got to know him better one found the man of rather excessive refinement trying with success to work like a day-laborer, deliberately hardening his skin to the burden, as though he were still carrying hides at Monterey" — this is absent/flattened in the draft. This is distinctive, voice-heavy prose.

13. "he set up a party of his own" — present.

14. The passage about the boy Henry's character: "Nature had given to the boy Henry a character that, in any previous century, would have led him into the Church; he inherited dogma and a priori thought from the beginning of time; and he scarcely needed a violent reaction like anti-slavery politics to sweep him back into Puritanism with a violence as great as that of a religious war." — The draft has this but omits "from the beginning of time" and "as great as that of a religious war" is present. Minor compression.

15. "A coarser instrument would have impressed them more. Average human nature is very coarse, and its ideals must necessarily be average." — absent from draft.

16. The passage about the father-son relationship in the context of the slave-power: "His father's business in life was to get past the dangers of the slave-power, or to fix its bounds at least. The task done, he might be content to let his sons pay for the pilotage; and it mattered little to his success whether they paid it with their lives wasted on battle-fields or in misdirected energies and lost opportunity." — This passage is entirely absent from the draft. This is interpretive weight material.

17. "The generation that lived from 1840 to 1870 could do very well with the old forms of education; that which had its work to do between 1870 and 1900 needed something quite new." — absent from draft.

18. The description of the boy's memory and school: "He thought his mind a good enough machine, if it were given time to act, but it acted wrong if hurried. Schoolmasters never gave time." — absent from draft.

19. The discussion of what the boy needed: "For success in the life imposed on him he needed, as afterwards appeared, the facile use of only four tools" — present.

20. "Henry Adams, as a brand escaped from the burning, always looked back with astonishment at their luck." — absent from draft.

Now let me assess severity:

- The pilotage/slave-power passage (#16) and the generations passage (#17) are interpretive weight material — high severity? Actually these are voice-establishing interpretive passages. The pilotage passage is distinctive and carries interpretive weight about the Adams family dynamic.

- The Dana "carrying hides at Monterey" passage is voice-establishing, prosodically distinctive — medium to high.

- "A coarser instrument would have impressed them more. Average human nature is very coarse" — voice-establishing, critical tradition passage.

- "Napoleons and Andrew Jacksons amuse it" — recognizable, somewhat famous.

- "He thought his mind a good enough machine, if it were given time to act, but it acted wrong if hurried. Schoolmasters never gave time." — voice-establishing, oft-quoted.

- "Henry Adams, as a brand escaped from the burning" — distinctive biblical allusion, voice.

- The pilotage passage — "it mattered little to his success whether they paid it with their lives wasted on battle-fields or in misdirected energies and lost opportunity" — this is interpretive weight.
